A2.text:
Gunel and Sevinj are students. They are roommates in a small flat in Baku. Gunel is very tidy. Sevinj is not. Her clothes are on the chairs, and her dishes are in the sink.

At first, they were friends. But after two months, Sevinj's mess started to bother Gunel. Small things can really get on someone's nerves.

Gunel did not want to argue. So she wrote notes and put them on the fridge. “Somebody forgot to wash her cup :)” “The bin is full — again!” The notes were passive-aggressive.

Sevinj was angry. She thought, “Gunel thinks I don't pull my weight.” She wrote her own note: “Somebody plays loud music at midnight :)”

For one week, they did not talk. The fridge was full of notes.

Then, one evening, Sevinj made tea and knocked on Gunel's door. “We need to clear the air,” she said.

They talked for two hours. Gunel said, “I need a clean kitchen. When you share a flat, you have to pull your weight.” Sevinj said, “I need quiet at night. I also need some privacy.”

They made a compromise. They wrote a list of chores. Every week, they split the jobs. Sevinj washes the dishes every evening. Gunel takes out the bin. And there is no music after eleven.

Now there is only one note on the fridge. It says: “Pizza night on Friday?”

B1.text:
When Gunel and Sevinj decided to share a flat near their university, everyone said it was a perfect match. They had been best friends since school and loved the same terrible Turkish series.

What nobody had considered was that Gunel was extremely tidy and Sevinj was not. Within a month, Sevinj's jackets lived on the chairs, her books covered the kitchen table, and her dishes stayed in the sink for days. Slowly but surely, the mess began to get on Gunel's nerves.

But Gunel hated arguments. So instead of saying anything, she started leaving small notes on the fridge. “Just a reminder: cups don't wash themselves :)” “The bin is full… again!” “Someone forgot it was her turn to buy bread :)” Each note had a smiley face. Each one felt like a slap.

Sevinj recognised passive-aggressive behaviour when she saw it, and she was hurt. Did Gunel really think she didn't pull her weight? She paid half the rent and did most of the shopping. So she answered with a note of her own: “Some people play music at 1 a.m. while others are trying to sleep :)”

For a week, the fridge door became a battlefield, and the two friends communicated only with sticky notes.

On Sunday evening, Sevinj made two glasses of tea, took a deep breath and knocked on Gunel's door. “This is ridiculous,” she said. “Can we clear the air?”

They talked until midnight. Gunel admitted that the mess made her anxious. Sevinj admitted that she needed more privacy and a quiet flat at night.

In the end, they made a compromise. They wrote a weekly list of chores and agreed to split them fairly: Sevinj would wash the dishes every evening and keep her things in her own room; Gunel would take out the bin and stop playing music after eleven.

The next morning, every sticky note had disappeared from the fridge except one, in Sevinj's handwriting: “Pizza on Friday? My treat.”

B2.text:
When Gunel and Sevinj announced they would share a flat near the university, everyone agreed it was a match made in heaven. Friends since primary school, studying the same degree and united by an unapologetic love of the same melodramatic Turkish series, they seemed incapable of falling out.

What nobody had factored in was that Gunel was fastidiously tidy and Sevinj cheerfully was not. Within a month, Sevinj's jackets had colonised the chairs, her textbooks had annexed the kitchen table and her dishes were taking extended holidays in the sink. Slowly but steadily, the mess began to get on Gunel's nerves.

Gunel, however, would rather walk barefoot on glass than have an argument. So instead of saying anything, she began leaving notes on the fridge. “Friendly reminder: cups don't wash themselves :)” “The bin is full… again!” “Someone forgot whose turn it was to buy bread :)” Every note ended with a smiley face, and every smiley face landed like a slap.

Sevinj knew passive-aggressive behaviour when she saw it, and she was wounded. Did Gunel genuinely believe she didn't pull her weight? She paid exactly half the rent and did nearly all the shopping. Her reply appeared the next morning: “Some people play music at 1 a.m. while others are trying to sleep :)”

For a week, the fridge door became a battlefield, and two lifelong friends communicated exclusively through yellow squares of paper.

On Sunday evening, Sevinj made two glasses of tea, steadied her nerves and knocked on Gunel's door. “This is absurd,” she said. “Can we please clear the air?”

They talked until well past midnight. Gunel confessed that clutter made her genuinely anxious. Sevinj confessed that she needed more privacy and silence at night. Both confessed that the notes had been a catastrophic idea.

What emerged was a compromise. They drew up a weekly rota of chores and agreed to split them fairly: Sevinj would wash up every evening and confine her belongings to her own room; Gunel would take out the bin and observe a strict no-music rule after eleven.

By the following morning, every note had vanished from the fridge except one, in Sevinj's looping handwriting: “Pizza on Friday? My treat. No smiley face required.”
